items.title: Sun
items.summary: The Sun, also known as Sol, is a star at the center of the solar system. It is a white star that gives off different types of energy such as infrared energy (heat), ultraviolet light, radio waves and light.

items.title: Moon
items.summary: The Moon, also known as Luna, is Earth's only natural satellite (the only object which orbits the Earth and is not man-made). It is usually visible in the night sky, but is sometimes seen during the day.

items.title: Mercury
items.summary: Mercury is the first planet from the Sun. It is the second hottest planet, and the smallest in the Solar System.

items.title: Venus
items.summary: Venus is the second planet from the Sun. Venus is the only planet in the Solar System that has a day longer than a year.

items.title: Mars
items.summary: Mars, also known as The Red Planet, is the fourth planet from the Sun and the second-smallest planet in the Solar System, after Mercury.

items.title: Jupiter
items.summary: Jupiter is the largest planet in the Solar System. It is the fifth planet from the Sun.

items.title: Saturn
items.summary: Saturn is the sixth planet from the Sun in our solar system. On average, Saturn is about 9.57 astronomical units (1,432 Gm; 1.432×109 km; 890,000,000 mi) away from the Sun.

items.title: Uranus
items.summary: Uranus is the seventh planet from the Sun in our Solar System. Like Neptune, it is an ice giant.

items.title: Neptune
items.summary: Neptune is the eighth and farthest planet from the Sun in the Solar System. It is an ice giant and the fourth-largest planet in the system.

items.title: Pluto
items.summary: Pluto is a dwarf planet in the Solar System with the formal name of 134340 Pluto and a planetary symbol , or . Pluto is the ninth largest body that moves around the Sun and the largest body in the Kuiper belt.

items.title: Solar System
items.summary: The Solar System is a group of space objects that are held together by gravity, with the Sun in the center. The Sun is a huge ball of hot glowing gas that gives off light and heat.

items.title: Milky Way
items.summary: The Milky Way is our home galaxy. It contains around 400 billion stars, including our Sun.

items.title: Galaxy
items.summary: A galaxy is a group of many stars, with gas, dust, and dark matter. The name 'galaxy' is taken from the Greek word galaxia meaning milky, a reference to our own galaxy, the Milky Way.

items.title: Star
items.summary: A star is a very large ball of bright, glowing, hot matter in space called plasma, which are held together by gravity. They emit light because they are very hot.

items.title: Black hole
items.summary: A black hole is a place in space where gravity is so strong that nothing can escape from it, even light. This idea comes from Albert Einstein's general theory of relativity.

items.title: Comet
items.summary: A comet is a ball of mostly ice that moves around in outer space. Comets are often described as "dirty snowballs".

items.title: Asteroid
items.summary: An asteroid is a minor planet that orbits within the inner solar system. It is a small object in the Solar System that travels around the Sun.

items.title: Solar eclipse
items.summary: As seen from earth, a solar eclipse /ee-klips/ happens when the moon is directly between the earth and the sun. This makes the moon fully or partially (partly) cover the sun.

items.title: Telescope
items.summary: A telescope (from the Ancient Greek τῆλε, tele "far" and σκοπεῖν, skopein "to look or see"; τηλεσκόπος, teleskopos) makes astronomical objects appear closer to the naked eye. It is an important tool for astronomy that gathers light and directs it to a single point.

items.title: Hubble Space Telescope
items.summary: Hubble Space Telescope (HST) is the first big optical space observatory telescope. Being above the atmosphere means it can see the sky more clearly than a telescope on the ground.

items.title: International Space Station
items.summary: The International Space Station (ISS) is a space station, a very large satellite that people can live in for several months at a time.

items.title: Apollo 11
items.summary: Apollo 11 was the first flight to send people to the moon. It was done by NASA, the American space group.

items.title: Yuri Gagarin
items.summary: Yuri Alexeyevich Gagarin (Russian: Юрий Алексеевич Гагарин; March 9, 1934 – March 27, 1968) was a Soviet and Russian cosmonaut (astronaut). He was the first person to travel into space.

items.title: Neil Armstrong
items.summary: Neil Alden Armstrong (August 5, 1930 – August 25, 2012) was an American astronaut, and engineer, and is known as the first person to walk on the moon. On July 20, 1969, Neil Armstrong and Buzz Aldrin landed on the moon in a small spacecraft that had been sent to the moon using the Saturn V rocket.

items.title: Space Shuttle
items.summary: The Space Shuttle was a spacecraft which was used by the American National Aeronautics and Space Administration, or NASA. Space Shuttles were used to carry astronauts and cargo into space.

items.title: Voyager 1
items.summary: Voyager 1 is a space probe launched by NASA on September 5, 1977, as part of a mission called the Voyager program to explore the outer Solar System and the space beyond our Sun's influence. It was launched shortly after its twin, Voyager 2.

items.title: Big Bang
items.summary: The Big Bang is a physical theory about how the universe started expanding, and then made the stars and galaxies we see today. The Big Bang is the name that scientists use for the most common theory of the universe, from the very early stages to the present day.

items.title: Supernova
items.summary: A supernova is the explosion of a giant star. It usually happens when the nuclear fusion in the star cannot hold the core against its own gravity.

items.title: Nebula
items.summary: A nebula is an interstellar cloud of dust, hydrogen, helium and other ionized gases in a galaxy.

items.title: Constellation
items.summary: A constellation is a group of stars which make up imaginary outline or pattern in the night sky (the celestial sphere). Usually they are said to represent an animal, mythological person or creature in a shape.
